name: Deep Livid Brown
lede: Deep Livid Brown is a dusty reddish brown from Ridgway's 1912 chart, using "livid" in its old sense of a leaden, bruised grey-red rather than the modern sense of furious.

sections.title: An old word for a bruise
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXIX gives this hue the name Deep Livid Brown, hue 1′′′, tone i, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the nearest category as "grayish red" in its block 19 [1]. *Livid* once meant simply a lead-grey, bruised color, from the Latin *lividus*; its modern sense of a person "livid with rage" is a later, figurative turn, and Ridgway's chart uses the older, plainer sense [1]. Its exact library match is [[faded-rosewood]], the same hex under a different name, a reminder that two dictionaries can arrive at one swatch from different directions [3].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 45, chroma 16, hue 28 degrees, Munsell 6.2R 4.4/3.1 [1]. The nearest distinct color is [[rose-taupe]], about 4.1 CIEDE2000 units away [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 204 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 0.86 percent, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1920s, in 10 of 237 paintings, at 4.9 times the overall rate, and is most loved by Mary Cassatt, in three of her seventeen paintings here, twenty-one times her own museums' baseline; it most often plays a mid-tone, in 49 percent of its appearances [4].

The earliest dated match is an untitled manuscript leaf from a Gandavyuha-sutra, the year 1000, nine centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
